title: Interstellar
title1: HOW CRUEL IS TIME: A REVIEW OF INTERSTELLAR
page1:
When I was a child, I loved the thought of growing up.
 Every time my parents yelled at me, grounded me, or pulled the classic “because I said so,” I would sit there furiously imagining the day when I would finally be bigger than them. Not physically bigger, necessarily, I just had a lot of ideas about adulthood. I sometimes dreamed that I had become a grown woman, smarter, stronger, independent, and nobody could order me around anymore. I wanted time to hurry up. Fast-forward ten years. Just get me out of here already.
 When you are a child, I often take time for granted. I stayed up through naps. I cannot wait for your next birthday. Adults keep warning me not to rush growing up, and obviously I ignore them because adults also tell you to eat vegetables and sleep before midnight, so their credibility is questionable.
But then I stumbled across and watched Interstellar.
It was a normal day, the weather was chilly but beautiful. I was sitting at home and I had a sudden urge to go out for a movie because it was such a beautiful day. My heart led me to the cinema with a friend, where we sat close to the IMAX screen and watched the whole 2 hours 49 minutes of Interstellar. Walking out of the door, we were so stunned that we did not talk to each other the whole way home.
page2:
Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar is about humanity trying to survive the apocalypse. Cooper, a former NASA pilot later becomes a farmer, leaves his children to travel through space in search of another habitable planet, perhaps to also satisfy his desire to go on an enormous adventure. Interested in the mystery of the universe from the start, extinction, galaxies, black holes, the fate of the human species raises my curiosity and forces me to focus deeply on the movie.
After that movie, I am afraid of time. When Cooper lands on Miller’s planet, the character knows that because of its proximity to the black hole Gargantua, time will move differently there, one hour on the planet equals roughly seven years back home, which is absolutely fascinating. After spending only a few hours on the planet, Cooper returns to the spacecraft and discovers that more than two decades have passed for everyone else on Earth. The video messages told him that his children had become adults, and some even gave up hope on waiting for him, they grow up in front of him through a screen.
It makes me sad watching Cooper sit there while years of his loved ones’ lives arrive one message after another. He has barely changed, yet the people he loves have birthdays, relationships, disappointments, families without him. The sounds and lighting of that scene was truly magnificent. I stared at the screen, mouth widened with shock when witnessing Christopher Nolan’s talent.
And for the first time, I found myself thinking about all those childhood nights when I begged the universe to make me older. What was I asking it to take away? We usually think of time as something that gives. Give it enough time and you will become wiser, more independent, more successful, heartbreak will heal, problems will pass. One day you will finally become the person you want to become. But Interstellar reminds us that time also takes, even more things that it gives. Cooper sacrifices the nurture of the relationship with his kids so that he can give them a future. Sometimes loving requires leaving the people we love, disappointing them or missing parts of their lives because of the bigger picture.
page3:
Strangely, the further Interstellar travels into the vast universe, the more it circles back to the most ordinary thing, which is family. Cooper’s entire journey is powered by his desire to return to his children. Murph spends much of her life carrying the influence of her father. Even when they are separated by distances that enormous, they continue to have an impact on each other’s life.
The people we love become part of us. We inherit their habits, sentences, fears, and courage. We leave home carrying much more of home. Humans travel across galaxies searching for another home, only to discover that “home” was always there. 
When I was little, I wished that I could grow up as fast as possible, but now I think time granted that wish too easily. Eight-year-old me did get her wish after all.

title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
title1: ETERNAL SUNSHINE OF THE SPOTLESS MIND: WOULD YOU ERASE SOMEONE YOU ONCE LOVED?
page1:
“How happy is the blameless vestal’s lot!
The world forgetting, by the world forgot.”
Have you ever wished you could just delete a person from your memory because just thinking about them is too painful? Perhaps you have laid awake at night, replaying an argument, a breakup, or one ordinary moment that suddenly became unbearable after someone left. But what if erasing the pain also meant losing every small moment that once made the relationship?
Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind answered this impossible question with one of the most painful love stories I have ever known. It was a gloomy Thursday in March, I was scrolling around, looking for something to do on an awfully tedious day and I accidentally came across this movie. I love the way its emotional depths linger, forcing us to confront our own memories and their complexities. 
The film follows Joel Barish, played by Jim Carrey, discovering his ex-girlfriend, Clementine Kruczynski, has undergone a medical procedure to erase all memories of their relationship. Hurt and humiliated, Joel decides to do the same. However, while the procedure is taking place, he is forced to revisit every moment in their relationship. As each memory disappears, Joel realizes that he does not truly want to forget Clementine after all.
page2:
At first, I expected the film to be a romantic drama about two incompatible people. Joel and Clementine are not an ideal couple. Clementine is impulsive, restless, and sometimes insensitive, while Joel often avoids conversations about his feelings and hides them. This relationship is messy because both of them are messy.  The movie does not treat love as a magical solution to problems like romantic comedies. On the other hand, the film challenges the idea that another person can complete us. Clementine has fears, impulses, and emotional wounds of her own.
The storytelling can be a little confusing and uncomfortable because the film moves through Joel’s collapsing memories as Joel fights against the procedure. Locations suddenly change, faces disappear, and objects become distorted. But honestly, are memories neat or chronological? We sometimes remember the feeling of a moment or the sound of someone’s voice, but forget their faces.
After a painful breakup, we may think the entire relationship as a mistake because that is easier than accepting that something can be so heartbreaking. Yet erasing pain does not get rid of its impact, forgetting does not free us, because love and pain goes so much deeper than memory. Regardless of how much we try to forget, we are always going to be drawn back to the feelings that made us who we are.
Maybe Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind does not support the idea that every relationship deserves another chance. Pain does not mean that love was meaningless. Because “Its better to have loved and lost than to never have loved at all.”
page3:
The ending is what stayed with me because it does not reveal that Joel and Clementine will become better people. They learn uncomfortable truths about each other and understand that they may repeat the same mistakes. Nevertheless, they choose to try again because they accept to love everything about the other person. Love is beautiful because even after seeing the risks, we still decide that love is worth it.
Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is strange, melancholic, humorous, and unexpectedly comforting. After watching this movie, I was left with one question: if I had the opportunity to erase someone who once broke my heart, would I actually do it? Honestly, I am not sure, and perhaps that is why the film remains so unforgettable.
Or maybe I can find my answer in Montauk.
“Let me keep this memory, just this one”.

title: Pearl
title1: PEARL: BEAUTIFUL, BUT NEVER THE MOST PRECIOUS JEWELRY
page1: This movie made me recognize myself in Pearl. Not in some “I could become a murderer” way. Absolutely not. I mean wanting people to notice you, feeling jealous when someone else gets the life you wanted, believing you deserve something bigger, or picturing a boring future thinking, there is no way this can be all I get.
page2:
Pearl lives on an isolated farm with her parents while her husband is away at war. Her life is everything she does not want: repetitive work, responsibility, feeling imprisoned and very little control over her life. She dreams of becoming a performer, she desires to dance. She wants people to look at her and say that she is special, she is a star. Who has not fantasized about escaping their boring life? Who has not imagined becoming successful so that everyone would look up to you? I understood that part.
She could tolerate being unhappy now because one day she would be famous. One day she would escape. One day everyone would notice her. One day all this suffering will only be the past. But what happens when “one day” never arrives? Pearl’s life is absolutely tragic. She has no backup plan, there is no version of her life where she is not dancing on a stage. So rejection and the realization that “maybe I was never special at all” is a much more throbbing wound. Mia Goth expresses the pain beautifully, especially during Pearl’s long confession near the end of the film. The scene lasts for several minutes and feels more intense than almost any other violence in the movie. Pearl just talks, and talks. The more she speaks, the worse it gets. What makes that scene extraordinary is that Mia fully portrays Pearl being exhausted, ashamed, jealous and resentful with her life. Pearl knows something is wrong with her and there are feelings she is not supposed to have. She knows she resents people she is also supposed to love. Underneath everything is the question: Why am I not happy?
Pearl’s mother is controlling, but she is not wrong when she warns Pearl about fantasizing her way out of reality. Pearl is trapped, but she also starts blaming everyone around her for the person she is becoming.
When watching protagonists, I like searching for the moment where they became bad. Was it their childhood? Their parents? Their loneliness? Rejection? Jealousy? What is special about this movie is Pearl does not give us one clean answer. Her pain builds up. A disappointment here, a humiliation there, someone else receiving the attention you wanted, feeling suffocated by reality. Together, they start building the emotional prison she eventually cannot escape. That is why I found myself feeling sorry for her, not because I supported what she did, but I can see why it is reasonable.
Pearl wants love, but she also wants admiration and freedom. She wants to escape the farm, but this is clearly not her biggest problem. You could put Pearl anywhere. If she still believed that being ordinary is living a tragic life, she would probably still be miserable.
page3: What I took from it is a feeling I could not name for a while. It is about how wanting something badly enough can stop being about the thing you want. I have seen it three times and it has not gotten softer, which I think is intentional.

title: Coraline
title1: TRUE OR FALSE: BETTER IS BETTER - A REVIEW OF CORALINE
page1:
I have probably replaced my own life in my head a thousand times. I would want something like a prettier room, more interesting people, parents who understand everything, a different house, a different city, a different version of myself and never have those painfully boring days. I do this often actually. Like whenever life becomes too repetitive, too disappointing, or too boring and not as exciting as I wanted it to be, my brain immediately imagines. What if everything was just a little more…perfect?
Before watching the movie, I knew Coraline through its reputation. A movie with creepy button eyes, strange stop-motion animation, a blue-headed girl crawling through a tiny door, a lot of theories from fans or one children’s movie that traumatized an entire generation. So I became curious.
page2:
Coraline Jones has recently moved into the Pink Palace Apartments with her parents, who are both very busy with their work. She is bored and lonely. But then Coraline finds a place behind a small door in her house, where another version of her world is located, but this world is better. Her Other Mother is attentive and the other Father is fun, the dinner is incredible, even the garden is created especially for her. Even the people she finds annoying in the real world become more lovely. Watching the first scenes, I thought that if I were Coraline, I would probably go back too. Obviously the button eyes are significant red flags, actually. But other than that, why not? The beldam is such an incredible villain because she lures children in by listening, watching, learning exactly what they dislike about their life.
The moment when the beldam makes her offer that Coraline can stay there forever, but with only one little condition. This part of the movie traumatizes all the children watching it, including me. All the earlier sweetness became horrifying. Coraline eventually had to pay the prices. The colourful fantasy starts collapsing, the Other Mother becomes increasingly frightening as she becomes more and more like a spider. The Other World only exists as long as Coraline desires it. Once she sees through it, everything begins to rot and fall. 
Eventually, Coraline returns to the same world she wanted to escape. Everything is the same, yet the place feels different. Maybe because Coraline is different, in her eyes, she does not see her world as awful as before and she started to appreciate the good things that are happening around her.
page3: I still think about a different scenario of my life in my head sometimes. But now there is occasionally one annoying image hiding somewhere in that fantasy. A tiny door, behind it, something smiling insidiously because it knows exactly what I want. That thought sends chills down my spine.

title: MAI
page1: I watched Mai because it had my name on the title. But halfway through the movie, I wished it didn’t. There is something uncomfortable about watching people shout your name while the woman is being humiliated, judged, abandoned, dragged back into her past so many times. Tran Thanh did take me from surprise to surprise.
page2:
Mai’s past follows her everywhere, her family takes from her, strangers judge her, people gossip about her, and even when she tries to keep her head down and struggles to make ends meet, somebody is always there to remind her about her horrible past. After a while, I stopped waiting for the story to get better and felt anxious every time Mai looked happy, because the movie had me expecting that something would come along and ruin it.
And this is probably where I became more emotionally involved than I expected. I felt truly sorry for her, that frustrating feeling where you start getting angry on behalf of a character. Mai makes questionable choices, shuts people out, and carries so much fear that she sometimes seems to sabotage the exact things she wants. But honestly, I understood that. If life has repeatedly taught you that good things come with a catch, why would you put down your guard?
Dương and Mai’s is not really amazing. Younger man, older woman, teasing and flirting, you can see right away that the connection is fragile. But Dương brings out a version of Mai that nobody else can. Around him, she jokes, gets embarrassed and she has the courage to stand up for herself. For a little while, their relationship feels like a romantic comedy.
The scene where Duong and Mai dance together in the bar hit me hard. It is cinematic and probably one of the scenes I remember most clearly. The music, the movement, the way Mai slowly lets herself become part of the moment, it is the most beautiful scene in this movie. What I loved is that for those few minutes, Mai became free and she looked so beautiful.
page3:
That is something “Mai” does incredibly well throughout the film. It takes things that seemed ugly, for instance scars, tired faces, emotional trauma and makes them tender. The movie finds beauty in places where it does not seem to exist.
Mai’s scars are still visible. Even Dương cannot rescue her from everything that came before him. The film lets Mai experience love but later tells her that love is not powerful enough. I think that romance movies make us used to the idea that if two people love each other, the universe eventually has to surrender. But Mai and Dương can love each other and still fail. Their feelings are real but still, they are not enough. They can meet at exactly the right moment to change each other and still meet at the wrong moment to build a life together. That was probably the part that haunted me the most. If Dương had stopped loving Mai, maybe I could have simply hated him. If Mai had stopped loving Dương, maybe the ending would have been easier to accept.
Sometimes love fails because it was not the right moment, someone comes into your life, teaches you some valuable lessons and then leaves anyway. There are so many moments where I kept thinking: will it be better for her if Mai was a man?
page4:
I cried while watching this movie partly because I felt sorry for Mai and I resonated with her exhaustion and the way she kept trying to be strong. That is why her moments of happiness felt so precious. Watching her laugh with Dương, dance, forget everything else makes me feel happy for them. 
The movie does not give Mai the future I hoped for her. I wished that after everything she has suffered through, fate would let this one thing work out for her. But reality is not that easy. 
I started watching because the main character happened to share my name. I did not expect to become protective of her, angry for her, embarrassed for her, hopeful for her, and eventually heartbroken for her. Moreover, I definitely did not expect a movie with my own name stamped across multiple times, making me think so much about scars, love, timing, and how cruel life can push what we truly want away.

title: Mamma Mia
title1: SLIPPING THROUGH MY FINGERS ALL THE TIME: MAMMA MIA!
page1:
Mamma Mia! made me question why I am not living on a Greek island, wearing white linen, dancing barefoot with my friends while singing an ABBA song. Everytime I watch Mamma Mia!, some part of me thinks: maybe I have been taking life too seriously.
I first watched the movie as a teenager, which was probably the perfect age for Sophie to become the character I understood most. She is young, restless, in love, about to get married. And for Sophie, she has to find her father so he can walk her down the aisle. She secretly reads Donna’s old diary, discovers three men, and invites all three of her mother’s ex-lovers to her wedding without telling anyone.
page2:
Sophie’s search for her father never felt to me like simple curiosity. She wants to know where she comes from before she decides where she is going. Finding her father will somehow make her feel more complete. Everything in Mamma Mia! is messy, but the movie keeps dancing and singing.
When I was younger, I mostly saw her as Sophie’s extremely energetic mother. Growing up made me realize Donna built everything on her own. She raised Sophie alone, ran the hotel, survived without a man, and created a home filled with people who love her deeply.
Donna is surrounded by friendship, memory, romance, regret, work, laughter. She still has unresolved feelings. She can handle years of raising a daughter alone and then completely fall apart because three men from her past have appeared at the same time.
Her friendship with Tanya and Rosie might be my favorite part of the entire movie. They are loud, ridiculous, and supportive. I absolutely loved watching women simply enjoy one another’s company.
This kind of relationship is more romantic than romance in Mamma Mia!. It is three women singing while running toward the sea.
“Dancing Queen” captures everything I love about the movie. Women drop what they are doing, join Donna, run through the village, dance on the pier, and suddenly an ordinary day becomes a musical. That is why I do not really care when people criticize Mamma Mia! for being cheesy. Because of course it is cheesy. That is the point of the movie.
The romance is also ridiculous, but charming and funny. Donna has three former lovers suddenly back in her life, Sophie is questioning whether she should even get married, everybody keeps misunderstanding everybody. Love in Mamma Mia! is also messy. That may be why the movie feels so free to me.
page3:
The scene that gets me emotionally is the famous “Slipping Through My Fingers.” Donna is helping Sophie prepare for the wedding, and she realized that her daughter is growing up. Donna has spent years raising Sophie, and now the little girl she remembers is standing in front of her as an adult preparing to build a life of her own. Sophie wants to discover the world. Donna once did exactly the same thing. She left, traveled, took risks. Now Sophie is standing at the same edge, and Donna has to do the incredibly difficult thing parents eventually have to do: let Sophie go and explore life on her own.
Somehow the movie feels nostalgic to me even though I do not have one specific childhood memory attached to ABBA. The music feels like a memory. ABBA songs sound euphoric and slightly sad at exactly the same time.
page4:
I watched Mamma Mia! because for roughly two hours, life looks free, spontaneous, sunny and fun. People get their hearts broken and keep dancing. Maybe not knowing exactly where your life is going is not a disaster.
Every time I finish Mamma Mia!, I want to go somewhere, travel the world, or maybe visit Greece immediately. I want sunlight, water, music, and people I love. Maybe that is the fantasy I keep returning to, the possibility of living a little more spontaneously and worrying a little less.
I know real life will never look exactly like Mamma Mia!. There will be no ABBA song playing whenever things go wrong. But I would still like to borrow something from that island, which is the willingness to be ridiculous and the confidence to start dancing.

title: AI - Artificial Intelligence
page1: I was 7 years old, going to my grandparents’ house, bored out of my mind, looking for something, anything to watch on the cable television. There was a channel called “Hollywood Classics”. I got to that channel exactly when. A.I. Artificial Intelligence started to play.
page2:
David is a highly advanced robotic child created to love. After Monica and Henry’s biological son becomes seriously ill, David is brought into their family as a substitute. He loves Monica with the innocence of a child. However, he existed and his ability to love was designed by humans.
Even when I was seven, something about that explanation did not make sense to me at all. If David’s love was only programmed, why did it hurt so much to watch? We usually think of robots as machines with no emotions whatsoever. Humans love, grieve, get attached, and make irrational decisions because somebody matters to us. Yet David spends his entire life trying to have somebody’s love although he is a robot.
David’s obsession with becoming a real boy hurts me so deep. He thought that if he finds the Blue Fairy from Pinocchio, she could transform him. After that, maybe he can become the child his mother chooses. 
When Monica abandons him, I understand why she does it. David has become dangerous within the family, especially after Monica’s biological son returns. Monica is placed in a difficult position between her biological child and David. 
During the Flesh Fair, obsolete robots are publicly destroyed for entertainment. The humans cheer while machines are burned and torn apart. When David appears, however, the crowd hesitates because he looks too much like a human, it becomes uncomfortable when the machine has a child’s face. That scene disturbed me so much because it reveals how horrible the people in the movie are.
page3:
After being abandoned, David becomes obsessed with the Blue Fairy. He suffers, travels because he still believes there is a magic spell that will make Monica love him again. He is offered other possibilities. But he only has one desire, which is being loved. When I first watched the movie, my seven-year-old mind thought that David’s love was real. I still think so. Perhaps his devotion began because someone designed it. However, humans are also shaped by childhood, family, culture, memory, fear, attachment, and thousands of experiences we went through in our lives. So why is David different? Is it because he is a robot? Can’t a robot learn to love and fight for that love?
At some point during A.I., I forgot he was artificial intelligence.And then comes the ending. David eventually finds an image of the Blue Fairy underwater and sits before her, wishing and asking again and again to become real. Time passes for roughly two thousand years, when human civilization disappears and the world changes completely. David still sits there, frozen inside the same wish. Two thousand years have gone by while one abandoned child continues waiting for his mother.
Eventually, the advanced beings who discover him reconstruct Monica for one final day. David finally gets what he yearns for. Monica wakes up beside him. They talk, play, celebrate his birthday, and spend the day together. She tells him she loves him. When I was seven, I cried when watching that scene from happiness because after everything he had endured, David finally got it. He has a mother and he is loved.
page4:
Humanity vanished, yet the love inside this robot remained stronger than time itself. Was that the evidence that his love was real, or the evidence that humans had created something powerful inside David? I still cannot find the answer to that question.
What began as a random film I watched because I was bored at my grandparents’ house became one of my earliest memories of feeling devastated for a character. After the credits, I remember thinking that everything David went through was so unfair. Even now, I still feel more sorry for him than I do for most of the humans in the movie. And perhaps that is the question A.I. Artificial Intelligence made me wonder all those years: if something can spend its entire existence loving, grieving, hoping, and refusing to let go, is it truly artificial?

title: Dead Poets Society
page1: Of course I wanted to choose my own future. Of course I wanted to make my own decisions without someone saying what is best for me. Freedom is beautiful - so, so beautiful - but the Dead Poets Society movie reveals Neil Perry’s tragedy while he chases that freedom.
page2:
Neil is intelligent, disciplined, popular, and has a future planned out for him to be successful. Neil is good at the life chosen for him. He could probably become the doctor his father wants. He could earn the degree, have a career, and make everyone proud. But does Neil actually want that life?
That was so frustrating. I think Mr. Perry loves his son so much that he wants what is best for Neil, and he believes he knows what is best. Neil’s father sees a successful future waiting for him and cannot understand why Neil would risk it for acting. To him, theatre is a distraction. But to Neil, it is possibly the only thing that makes him feel free.
As I watch him perform as Puck, Neil looks happier than he does at any other point in the film, and the audience already knows that this happiness is temporary. He has found something that makes him feel alive, but he has not found the freedom to keep it.
Mr. Keating gives Neil something his father never really does, which is imagining another life. “Carpe Diem” sounds intoxicating when Keating first introduces it. Seize the day. Think for yourself. Refuse to become whatever the world has decided you should be. I loved his philosophy, but I also think the movie exposes its limits. Keating can teach the boys to look at life differently, but he did not tell them about the consequences when they cannot control themselves.
page3:
That is why I do not blame him for Neil’s death, though I cannot say his influence meant nothing. Keating opened the door. The tragedy is that Neil discovered freedom before he had the maturity to deal with the cost that comes along with it.
Neil’s death makes “Carpe Diem” heavier for me. Seizing your life requires more than courage.. It is easy to tell someone to choose themselves. It is much harder when choosing yourself might mean losing your family’s approval, changing the future everyone has imagined for you, or accepting that freedom comes with consequences you cannot neatly control.
The friendships between the boys make all of this more painful. Neil is surrounded by people who love him, yet none of them fully understands how desperate he has become. Todd especially makes the ending unforgettable. When he finally stands on his desk and says, “O Captain! My Captain!”, I felt pride, goosebumps, and grief at the same time. It is technically an act of gratitude, but more importantly, it is Todd finally making a choice that belongs entirely to him.
And still, it changes nothing. In reality, Neil is gone. Keating still has to leave.

title: Adventure Time
page1:
“Come down for dinner!”
“Eleven more minutes mom”
My parents could call my name from the other room for the third time. If Adventure Time had just started, then whatever was happening could survive on their own until Finn and Jake were done fighting some horrifying monster made of candy or singing about something that made absolutely no sense. Back then, the show was eleven colorful minutes of weird jokes and bizarre creatures. I had no idea I was watching stories about war, abandonment, heartbreak, and death.
I started watching Adventure Time when I was very young, mostly because it was funny. There were candy people, Marceline, talking clouds, and Ice King. And of course there was a kingdom made of candy.
When rewatching parts of the show when I was older, I began realizing how much had been happening right in front of me.
page2:
As a child, Ice King was the annoying villain who kidnapped princesses because he desperately wanted someone to marry him. He was ridiculous and irritating. Then Adventure Time shows us who he used to be. Simon was once a normal man. But the magical crown that saved him also gradually destroyed his memory and personality until almost everything that made Simon Simon disappeared.
The relationship between Marceline and Simon is probably the part that stuck with me. During the aftermath of the Mushroom War, Simon becomes a father figure to Marceline when she is still a child. He protects her in a destroyed world even while he knows the crown is slowly taking him away from himself. Fast forward to the present, Marceline remembers Simon even when Simon can barely remember himself. As a child, I could not have understood why that was frightening. Adventure Time became much sadder when I grew up.
Finn begins as this wildly enthusiastic kid. And strangely, I love him more as he grows older. He falls in love and then gets rejected. He also makes mistakes, hurts people. Sometimes his belief got shattered into pieces. But Finn keeps loving people anyway. That is one of the things I admire most about him. There are a million reasons to become cynical, and somehow he never does. His optimism is still there, he is still childish and fun.
When I was little, I wanted things to be exactly the same. I did not think about childhood ending. Cartoon Network will always be there in the afternoon. I have a strong desire to return to a simpler version of life. Sometimes I miss childhood because of that.
page3:
Under all the candy kingdoms and magical creatures lies the remains of our own world after an apocalyptic war. As a child, I barely noticed. Now I think that is one of the most beautiful ideas in the series. Something catastrophic happened, and life did not return to what it was before but became something else much more beautiful.
I do not remember the finale well enough to cry and say goodbye to a part of my childhood. My goodbye to Adventure Time was that I simply stopped watching regularly at some point. I just grew up and got busy with life. One afternoon became another. Eventually, those eleven minutes that once seemed important to me so much that I have to delay dinner became memories.
page4:
Maybe the final time I watched Adventure Time as a child, somebody called me to eat and I complained that I needed eleven more minutes. Now when I return to the show, I still laugh. I still love the stupidity, the weird characters, and its world does not work normally. But somewhere behind all of it, I can see Simon losing himself as Marceline still remembers him and waiting for him to remember her, Finn grows older and Ooo rebuilding itself over the ruins.
Still, if you offered me one completely ordinary childhood afternoon again, Cartoon Network playing in the background, dinner ready, somebody calling my name from the other room. Then I would know exactly what I would ask for.
“Just eleven more minutes.”

title: Better Days
page1: I thought Better Days was a sad coming-of-age film. But it felt suffocating watching two teenagers try to survive this cruel world.
page2:
Chen Nian is preparing for the gaokao, the exam that determines everything about her future. Every student here believes in the promise that if they can get through this exam, better days will come afterward. Apart from stress from the academic work, she is bullied by her classmates and suffers trauma from her family.
Because she endured too much on her own, it frustrated me and made me feel protective of her. I wanted to scream at the screen for her to tell someone everything or she could just scream or fight back. There are the girls who actively torment Chen Nian, but there are also the people watching, the students who know and the adults who can see what is happening. The cruelty in Better Days is silence.
Then Xiao Bei appears. To be honest, he is not an ideal person that Chen Nian should rely on. He usually gets into fights and looks like danger. But underneath all that roughness is an almost tenderness, especially toward Chen Nian. Their bond is beautiful but also tragic. Two lonely souls meet when they need each other the most.
“You protect the world, and I’ll protect you.”
Chen Nian wants to study and have a better life than what she has now. On the other hand, Xiao Bei has already been pushed outside society, he does not have an academic path, but he can give her the reassured feeling that there is somebody who is watching out for her. Chen Nian has a potential future while Xiao Bei has almost nothing.
page3:
The contrast between his appearance and his behavior surprised me. He looks intimidating, and often treated as trash by society. But around Chen Nian, there are moments of softness.
At the end of the movie, after everything they have been through, Xiao Bei sacrificed for Chen Nian. There is something beautiful about the act of sacrificing for someone you love. But in this case, it felt sad and suffocating. Xiao Bei is willing to give up almost everything for Chen Nian. He is willing to become the bad person everyone assumes he is if it means she gets the life that she wants and the future she desires. 
Their situation feels so unfair. Life keeps placing them in circumstances where they cannot be happy. Chen Nian’s future matters, but so does Xiao Bei’s. Her education matters, but so does his life.
One minute, you are watching something vicious to make you angry at all the characters. Then suddenly there is a small moment between Chen Nian and Xiao Bei that feels heartwarming. He follows behind her, protecting her like he promised. They can just sit together comfortably without having to say anything to one another.
Those moments are when they can relax and it seems like nothing else in the world matters. The flow slowed down, escaping from the hustle and bustle, there were just two people finally finding peace in one another.
page4:
Better Days is also about loneliness, class, academic pressure, guilt and love.
The bullying theme made me ask questions in my head about when isolation becomes harassment, when harassment becomes violence and by the time an adult finally understands the full situation, how much damage has already been done?
The film does show us hope in this situation after all, but I would not call the ending comforting. I felt more relieved. I was glad Chen Nian and Xiao Bei still found light at the end of the tunnel. But I was also angry that they had to suffer so much before receiving hope for a better future. I wanted better days for them, but I hated the price they had to pay to reach them.
Better Days. The phrase sounds hopeful. It is true that eventually things will get better.
But Chen Nian should not have needed Xiao Bei to become her bodyguard, she should have a normal life like any other students. Chen Nian and Xiao Bei’s relationship is so beautiful. When nobody else cares, they can find comfort in each other.

title: Spider-Man: No Way Home
page1: I’ve been a Marvel fan since forever. I read the comics first, then watch every movie of the MCU. So by the time Spider-Man: No Way Home arrived at the theatre, I was so excited that I brought the tickets to the early screening. I wanted to know what will happen to the friendly Spiderman on the screen, and the movie can bring me back to my childhood.
page2:
When Andrew Garfield walked through that portal, the whole theatre screamed and I got goosebumps. I basically went through the full emotional range of a devoted Marvel fan in about fifteen seconds. The internet had spent months analyzing blurry pictures and interviews so I knew there was a strong possibility that Andrew and Tobey would appear.
Andrew’s return hit me especially hard because The Amazing Spider-Man was the version I had loved most growing up. He was always my Spider-Man because he is too cool. We become attached to fictional characters because we attach them to ourselves. A particular costume, theme song, or stupid line suddenly contains an entire period of your life. So when Marvel brought back characters from previous Spider-Man films, I was living in my childhood life when I first loved them.
The story begins with Peter Parker suffering the consequences of having his identity exposed to the world. His solution is to ask Doctor Strange to cast a spell to make everyone forget about him. But as Strange changes the spell so many times, people from other universes begin appearing, and Peter realizes that the villains who have crossed into his world are being sent back to their world where many of them are destined to die. With a heart full of kindness, Peter refuses and he tries to save them, even if doing so creates more danger for himself. Doctor Strange tells him that these deaths are their fate, but Peter still cannot accept sending someone toward death when there might be another solution.
And for that kindness, he gets absolutely destroyed. Aunt May dies. His life collapses around him because he tried to help people who were not his responsibility. But “with great power comes great responsibility”. I knew something terrible was going to happen, but Aunt May’s death still hurt. After everything, Peter becomes angry and wants revenge. The boy who believed that every villain deserves another chance is ready to kill Norman Osborn.
page3:
In this movie, Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin is terrifying, maybe even more frightening than he was twenty years earlier. Dafoe’s expression does all the work. Each time he speaks or laughs, the voice sends chills down my spine. For a moment, I actually believe Peter will beat him to death at the end of the movie. But Tobey stops him with just a serius look with a head shake. Just one Spider-Man standing between another Spider-Man and a decision he knows Peter will regret. Tom is about to discover what loss can turn him into. But Andrew already knows and Tobey has lived with it long enough to understand.
Andrew, especially, carries his grief so openly. When he talks about Gwen, it feels like he has never completely forgiven himself. He admits that after losing her, he stopped “pulling his punches”. That small confession says so much about the Spider-Man we never got to see after The Amazing Spider-Man 2. He kept being Spider-Man, but his heart was broken after the death of the love of his life. So when MJ falls from the Statue of Liberty, everyone watching knows that it is referencing the fall from The Amazing Spiderman movie. Andrew dives, he catches her and then he looks at her with an expression that completely ruined me. He is looking at MJ and seeing the person he could not save. He cannot bring Gwen back. But this time, he learned from his mistakes, not relying on his web and successfully saved MJ.
Marvel absolutely knows what they are doing. It knows we want the pointing meme, the old villains, Tobey talking about his back, Andrew being called amazing. But other than those crowd-pleasing moments, Doctor Octopus gets another chance, Andrew catches MJ, Tobey stops a person from making the mistake he once made.
page4:
That final spell is probably the cruelest choice the film could have made. Everyone forgets Peter Parker. When Peter walked into the coffee shop afterward, I desperately wanted him to tell them. Explain everything. But he sees that they are doing well and he leaves. That moment is where Tom Holland’s Peter finally becomes the Spider-Man I recognize from the comics. Spider-Man has always been a hero built around sacrifice. Peter Parker can save everyone else’s relationship and ruin his own. He can also do the right thing and receive absolutely nothing in return. But he still puts the suit back on and continues to be the friendly neighbour Spider-Man.
I was surprised because of how much the movie reminded me why I loved Marvel so much in the first place.
Nostalgia is powerful because returning to something you once loved lets you meet the person you were when you loved it for the first time. For me, Tobey carries one era of Spider-Man, Andrew carries another, and Tom carries the present. Seeing them together felt like three versions of myself at three different times in my life standing in the same frame.
And if No Way Home was Marvel paying homage to twenty years of Spider-Man on screen, then this is mine: Thank you, Tobey, for showing me who Spider-Man was. Thank you, Andrew, for making me love him. And thank you, Tom, for reminding me why Peter Parker keeps being Spider-Man, even when it costs him everything.

title: Little Woman
page1:
There is a cousin of mine whom I have always thought of more like a sister. When we were younger, we did not have to schedule anything or ask what had changed since the last time we saw each other. But as we grow up, we have different routines, different priorities that make us grow apart. Watching Little Women makes me feel sadder about this.
The March house is noisy, chaotic, crowded, and affectionate. They fight over ridiculous things, steal each other’s belongings and somehow always end up back around the same table. Watching those scenes, I thought about how ordinary all of it was, and how ordinary things are usually not appreciated until they stop.
page2:
Jo was the character I resonate with most. She loves freedom as much as myself. Marriage, expectation, convention, even love seems dangerous because she is terrified of being held back. She wants to write and earn her own money. Most importantly, she wants the right to decide her future. I loved that about her. Jo refuses marriage because she knows she does not love Laurie in the way he wants her to. I completely understand that decision. But somehow I still wanted them together. Their chemistry, their friendship, the way they understand each other, it makes the rejection hurt even when I know Jo is right.
That scene where Jo says she is tired of people thinking “love is all a woman is fit for”, and then admits that she is lonely, is probably the moment that hits me. Both things can be true. A woman can reject the idea that marriage is a lack of freedom and still want to be loved. 
I know Jo is the sister I naturally gravitated toward, but Amy’s talk about marriage stayed in my head. For women of her time, women like her are affected by whom she marries. “I want to be great or nothing” was a bold claim. Amy was a strong woman. She does not simply want to paint because painting makes her happy. She wants excellence. She knew that she may never become the great artist she imagined herself becoming. Rather than romanticizing her struggle, she reconsiders what she wants in life.
Meg especially surprised me. I thought of her as the sister who settled, particularly beside Jo’s fierce ambition. Her famous line “Just because my dreams are different does not mean they are less important”. She genuinely wants the life of having a family of her own. Emma Watson's appearance was what drew me to this movie in the first place. Although being a small character, she portrayed Meg’s personality beautifully.
Beth does not have Jo’s ambition or Amy’s determination to become great. She is quieter, gentler with the people around her. Her absence eventually changes the entire family. Watching Jo understand that she cannot save Beth hurt me more than Beth’s illness. Jo is a person who deals with problems by fighting, writing, fixing them by her own hand. But this time, she can only lose her. And after Beth, the March house never feels quite the same.
page3:
The movie brought me back to my own cousin. Nothing tragic has happened between us. We just grew apart. People move on to separate lives. And I begin yearning for the old memories and nostalgia. Little Women shows that grief beautifully. Growing up is gaining independence and watching everyone you grew up with gain theirs too. Jo becomes a writer, Amy builds a different future, Meg has her family. Life moves forward. But moving forward means the sisters cannot be those four girls crowded inside one house forever.
In the publishing sequence, Jo finally sees her book produced, watches her name become something tangible, and owns the work she fought to create. I still admire Jo for wanting a life that belonged to her. I still wish that Jo and Laurie could somehow have worked. But at the same time, I understand Amy more than I expected. I respect Meg and her dreams. And Beth makes me want to pay more attention to the people around me.
Maybe that is what Little Women made me realize that I should love people while they are still close to me. Because one day, we will all grow up. And someday you may look back at the noisy room where everybody used to be together with nostalgia.

title: Seven (1995)
page1:
Everything in Se7en is wet, dark, dirty and looks like it smells terrible. There is barely a moment where the movie lets you feel comfortable, and after a while I started feeling like I had been locked inside that city with them. That is what makes Se7en so disturbing. John Doe does horrible things, but he is calm and he has thought about everything carefully. Even worse, some of what he says about people, their greed, cruelty, indifference, obsession with themselves, is undeniably true. His conclusions are monstrous, and his mindset is disturbing, but the dark side he sees in people is not ridiculous.
That bothered me far more than the seven deadly sins themselves. Gluttony, greed, sloth, lust, pride, they are horrifyingly transformed into murders, but John Doe is not really interested in punishing. He has appointed himself the judge to make people become disillusioned. The scariest part is that he believes his moral compass is more accurate than everyone else’s.
page2:
Somerset seems to understand this darkness. He has seen enough ugliness that he no longer expects much from people. Mills is the opposite. He is emotional and impatient but still has hope for the world to be better. I related more to that emotional side of him, and I increasingly felt sorry for him because John Doe understands how Mills thinks.
Then Tracy brings warmth into Se7en. Her presence gives Mills a home, a wife, an ordinary life. In retrospect, that is horribly important because John Doe does not simply want to murder people around Mills. He wants to destroy the ordinary life that makes Mills human.
I watched the ending completely blind, which I am very grateful for.
By the time Doe takes Somerset and Mills into the desert, I knew something terrible was coming. Still, I could not work out what he wanted or what he was going to do until the box arrived. Somerset understands what is happening while Mills doesn’t. Watching that realization move across Somerset’s face while Mills keeps asking what is happening created a level of dread that none of the earlier murders managed to match.
When Mills finally knew what was in the box, I desperately wanted him not to pull the trigger. John Doe has murdered Tracy in the most brutal way, reveals that she was pregnant, and then stands in front of Mills telling him to kill him. To avenge his beloved wife, Mills wants to shoot John. The audience knows that revenge is exactly what Doe wants, he wants to prove that no matter what happens, Mills cannot control the anger burning inside his heart at the moment.
page3:
He is the last one in the seven deadly sins, which is wrath.
That reveal completely changed my perspective. I was shocked, because of how brutal and smart this plan is. The drive into the desert was the detectives walking right into Doe’s trap. Even his death had already been planned.
I still cannot decide whether John Doe truly wins. Mills gives him what he wants, and the seven sins are completed. But everyone is destroyed by the end, including Doe himself. There is nothing triumphant about it. Se7en left me wondering how people continue believing in the world and hope for it to become better. The movie never gives me an answer.
It just keeps raining.

title: Before Sunrise
page1: I sometimes think about how many people I have probably walked past without knowing they could have mattered to me. Someone on a train, someone waiting for coffee, someone sitting two seats away while I was too busy checking my phone or thinking about where I needed to be next. Most of those people were probably just strangers, obviously. But Before Sunrise made me entertain the ridiculous possibility that maybe one of them could have changed my life if I had just looked up at the right moment.
page2:
That is basically what happens to Jesse and Céline. They meet on a train in Europe, start talking, and then Jesse asks her to get off with him in Vienna. When he asks, I completely understand why Céline says yes. There is something irresistible about stepping outside your plans for once and seeing what happens. Just one night and in a strange city.
I was taken aback by how deep their connection is despite how fast it happens. Their relationship developed through smallI talks and deep conversations. They walk around Vienna discussing love, death, parents, relationships, ridiculous little observations about strangers, and things they probably would not tell people they actually know. Somewhere between all those conversations, the attraction becomes obvious.
Céline was the character I connected with more. She can be romantic and skeptical at the same time. She talks seriously about love but is also aware of how strange this entire situation is. I liked that contradiction because it keeps their night from becoming too perfect. She questions Jesse, disagrees with him, teases him, and figures out what she believes while saying it.
page3:
The café scene where they pretend to call their friends was probably my favorite. It is such a simple idea, but it captures everything awkward and exciting about liking someone before you are willing to admit that you like them. They are talking to imaginary people, but it is obvious that they are really talking to each other. They can say things they would feel ridiculous saying directly. It is playful, slightly embarrassing, and somehow more intimate because they both know exactly what they are doing.
Before Sunrise does not make romance depend on enormous gestures. Jesse and Céline just keep talking until you start feeling that deep and sacred bond. Their conversations wander the way real conversations do. Something philosophical turns into something stupid, something funny becomes personal.
I think that is why I believe their connection, even if I also think something like this probably happens very rarely. The fact that they do not know each other well may actually help. They do not need to worry about what the other person will think six months later because, as far as they know, there may not be a six months later. That gives the night an honesty. They can become versions of themselves that exist only for each other.
And Vienna makes everything feel even more unreal. They wander through streets, sit in cafés, look across the city, and slowly make an ordinary night feel like some private world that will disappear once morning arrives. I loved that dreamlike quality. Vienna belongs to neither of them. But of course, time is exactly what makes the night special. If Jesse and Céline knew they had more time together, they might not talk the same way. Instead, knowing the night will end makes everything more intense.
Before Sunrise gives me nostalgia for something I have never actually experienced.
I have had conversations that became unexpectedly personal very quickly, and I would rather keep those memories vague, but I understand the strange feeling of realizing that someone you barely know has suddenly been allowed into a part of your mind that people who have known you much longer have never seen.
page4:
The ending could easily have broken the movie for me, but instead it made me feel hopeful. When Jesse and Céline say goodbye and agree to meet again six months later, I want to believe them completely. I know how unrealistic that probably is. Nothing, just faith that both of them will return to the same place on the same date. But maybe that is exactly why I loved it. Part of me wanted them to stay together right then. Another part knew that extending the night might ruin what made it special in the first place. Nothing is guaranteed, but it does not feel over.
That feeling stayed with me more than anything else is the certainty I somehow had that they would see each other again.
Maybe that is also why Before Sunrise made me think about strangers differently. It reminded me how much of life depends on tiny decisions that seem completely meaningless. Most of those moments probably lead nowhere. Occasionally, they lead to Vienna.
And after Before Sunrise, I cannot help wondering how many times I have walked straight past mine.
